newsitem.title: JAPAN: Chase Manhattan says more Japan mergers unlikely.
newsitem.headline: Chase Manhattan says more Japan mergers unlikely.

text.p: Japan's "Big Bang" financial deregulation plan may encourage some Japanese financial institutions to merge with foreign counterparts, but a great rise in cross-border mergers is unlikely, the managing director of Chase Manhattan Bank in Tokyo said.

"Mergers are not an easy thing to pull off... It takes considerable time, patience, and the right kind of mindset," Robert Fallon, head of the Asia-Pacific Division of Chase Manhattan Bank in Tokyo, told Reuters in an interview.

In the wake of the business tie-up between Bankers Trust New York Corp and Nippon Credit Bank Ltd (NCB) in April, some small Japanese financial institutions may begin to look for foreign "big brothers" to survive a possible industry shake-out, he said.
But he doubted this would become a trend.
"I don't see that (acquisition of Japanese banks by foreign banks) as a likelihood... The general environment is that these cross-border acquisitions are culturally challenging."
Asked if Chase Manhattan is considering a major tie-up with a Japanese financial institution, Fallon said: "It's not something that I would rule out categorically, but I would say it's unlikely."

Bankers Trust and Nippon Credit Bank announced in April they had agreed on a business tie-up under which the U.S. bank would securitise some of NCB's loans and help maintain services to NCB customers after the Japanese bank's planned withdrawal from overseas operations.
But Fallon added that the number of the Japanese banks may be reduced once deregulation takes place.

"Frankly, in Japan there are too many banks, probably too many insurance companies. And all this leads to consolidation (as a result of the deregulation)," he said, adding that the stronger players in the market would eventually take over the weaker ones.

Under the Big Bang plan announced by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto in November, Japan aims to liberalise its financial markets by 2001 to catch up with reforms carried out more than a decade ago in Europe and North America. Ministry panels are expected to announce details in June.

Fallon said the deregulation should provide more opportunities for foreign financial institutions and may encourage those who have moved their regional headquarters to Singapore or Hong Kong over the past several years to return.

Deregulation could create an attractive international capital market in Japan, while allowing foreign financial institutions to compete with domestic rivals by providing more innovative products in the areas of international cash management and trading risk mitigation systems, he said.
The foreign firms could also offer sophisticated electronic banking services such as automated trade processing and expertise in derivatives trade, he added.

But Fallon said that in order to make the planned deregulation a more successful initiative, more efforts are needed by the Ministry of Finance to ensure greater disclosure and to liberalise the tax environment.
